about: What the `lua` selection of SCE_SCRIPT_ENGINE answers differently from
ECMA-262, case by case, against the shared table beside this file.
The engine that selection reaches is Lua 5.4 with
`EcmaScriptToLuaTransformer` rewriting the author's ECMAScript into Lua
text. It is a listed, validated value of the cache entry, so a consumer
may build with it; the default is `quickjs`, which answers every case in
the shared table.
This file exists because the count used to live in prose. A comment said
26 of 58 on the day someone measured it, the shared table then grew to 98
cases, and nothing re-answered the question: the real number on
2026-08-18 was 44. A list the test reads cannot drift that way. An entry
here that starts agreeing fails as loudly as a case that starts
disagreeing, so neither direction passes unnoticed.
`needs` says what closing an entry would take, and it is nearly the same
answer every time:
operand-boundaries  A rewriting pass replaces text without knowing
where an operand ends. `a && b` cannot yield its
left operand, `1 == '1'` cannot coerce, and
`-7 % 3` cannot truncate, because no pass can say
what `a`, `1` or `-7` extend to. Closing these
means parsing the expression, which SCE already
does once, in the build-time frontend that every
generated backend shares.
chain-operand       The operand of a prefix operator is the whole
member and call chain after it, not the first name
in it.
statement-structure A statement form the script pipeline does not read.
The divergences that were not of that kind have been repaired rather than
listed: member calls the shared runtime library already defined, a string
literal no pass could see as a receiver, a computed index that was never
shifted, `Math.round`, and `\uXXXX`. Those took 44 disagreements to 23.
`diverges_on` says WHICH PATH into the engine the entry is about, and it
is the field that lets this list empty. `needs` says what closing an
entry would take — a cause. It does not say where the entry is still
wrong, and there are two different code paths that reach the same Lua:
runtime-rewriter     The generated artifact hands the engine the
AUTHOR'S ECMAScript and `EcmaScriptToLuaTransformer`
rewrites it on the spot. Held two-directionally by
`ecmascript_semantics_test`.
build-time-lowering  `sce-build`'s ECMAScript frontend emitted Lua and
the artifact hands the engine that, so the rewriter
is never reached. Held two-directionally by the
`LoweredEcma262` suite, which asks the WHOLE shared
table rather than this list — a path's divergences
cannot be enumerated by a list built from the other
path's.
So an entry stays here while ANY path still answers it differently, and
it LEAVES when `diverges_on` would be empty. That is the emptying this
list previously had no shape for: with one unmarked population, an entry
could only go when the rewriter was repaired, and the plan of record is
to RETIRE the rewriter for generated code rather than repair it. Marked
per path, the build-time column is a number that reaches zero on its own
terms, and each list's suite is red both ways — an undeclared divergence
and a declared one that has been repaired fail alike.
`paths` below is the set an entry may name, and it is not decoration: a
value naming a path nothing measures would be a claim no lane can fault.
`ecma262_scoreboard_contract` compares it against what `sce-build`
derives for this backend (`Language::supports_script_engine_target`), so
the day C++ gains or loses a path, this key and the entries under it are
held to the change instead of outliving it.
